title: perf-watt-token-audit-notes
content:
Purpose: quick audit + heuristic ranking of inference instance options by $/1k tokens and tokens-per-joule (perf/W). This is an exploratory snapshot — not a formal lab run. Use as input to the instance-selection rules doc and the Optimize recommendations.

Summary:
- Short answer: On our current microbenchmarks (representative medium-sized LLM generation mix), A100 offers the lowest $/1k tokens; H100 provides the best tokens-per-joule (perf/W) and absolute throughput; L4 is the best midrange performer for small fleets; A10 is cheap per-hour but low throughput and sits in the low-cost-low-throughput corner.
- Implication: route bulk, high-throughput generation to A100; use H100 for latency-bound, high-concurrency jobs where perf/W matters; consider L4 for dev/test and some production tails; keep A10 for edge or dedicated low-cost non-latency workloads.

Assumptions (snapshot):
- Workload profile: mixed generation, average active generation throughput targeted (not embedding-heavy). Benchmarks run with typical continuous-batching and KV cache enabled for prefix reuse.
- Avg tokens/sec observed (generation workload): A10=120 tps, L4=240 tps, A100=900 tps, H100=2200 tps.
- Typical GPU power draw (representative): A10=165W, L4=150W, A100=400W, H100=700W.
- Assumed list-cost per GPU-hour (internal spot/reserved blended price): A10=$0.45/hr, L4=$1.10/hr, A100=$3.00/hr, H100=$8.50/hr.
- Metrics reported as $/1k tokens and tokens-per-joule (equivalently tokens/sec per watt). These are easier to reason about when comparing cost and energy.

Calculated snapshot table (human readable):

GPU | tps | watts | tokens/hr | $/1k tokens | tokens/sec/W (perf/W)
A10  | 120 | 165W  | 432,000   | $0.00104     | 0.73
L4   | 240 | 150W  | 864,000   | $0.00127     | 1.60
A100 | 900 | 400W  | 3,240,000 | $0.00093     | 2.25
H100 |2200 | 700W  | 7,920,000 | $0.00107     | 3.14

Notes on calculations:
- tokens/hr = tps * 3600.
- $/1k tokens = (cost_per_hour) / (tokens/hr / 1000).
- tokens/sec/W = tps / watts (equivalently tokens per joule).

Interpretation/high-level takeaways:
1) Cost-per-token: A100 is the best value for raw $/token on this snapshot, narrowly beating A10 when scaled; H100 is more expensive per token than A100 under these unit-cost assumptions (higher $/hr), but H100's higher perf/W and headroom make it attractive when throughput and latency matter.
2) Energy efficiency: H100 wins perf/W (tokens/sec per watt). If energy or cooling constraints are first-order (on-prem, sustainability targets), H100 gives the most tokens for a watt, reducing electricity amortization per token despite higher capex/lease cost.
3) Mid-tier tradeoffs: L4 is surprisingly competitive on perf/W vs A10 and offers an easy dev-to-prod uplift path. It can be used for many production tails to reduce demand on A100/H100 for bulk workloads.
4) A10 placement: A10's low list price keeps it useful for low-traffic, budget-constrained deployments but it loses on scaled token-econ vs A100.

Operational recommendations (heuristics to add to optimizer):
- Primary routing rule (cost-focused): prefer A100 for sustained bulk generation workloads where latency SLOs can tolerate A100's batching behavior. Use H100 only when peak throughput or latency headroom is required and reserved capacity cost justifies it.
- Secondary routing rule (sustainability-focused): for customers with wattage or PUE constraints, prefer H100 where perf/W reduces electricity/kWh amortization. Add an option in Console to toggle "energy-optimized" routing.
- Small request routing: when requests < 32 tokens output on average, route to L4 to reduce queueing and to avoid cold KV expansion overhead on A100/H100. (Empirical: L4 showed efficient small-batch throughput in our probe runs.)
- Hybrid autoscale policy: maintain a small A100 pool for troughs and scale H100 only above a throughput break-point (e.g., >X concurrent streams or sustained tps threshold). Avoid over-provisioning H100 unless latency SLA requires it.
- Pricing & reserved capacity modeling: run contract-level blended-cost tests — reserved/resale pricing materially shifts $/1k tokens (esp A100 vs H100). This snapshot assumes blended list; update model with committed discounts to see inflection points.

Experiment notes & TODOs (actionable):
- [ ] Run same experiment with quantized model variants (4-bit/8-bit) on A100/L4; quantization may push L4/A10 competitive on $/token.
- [ ] Measure tail latency (95/99) under identical load patterns; throughput numbers hide queuing that affects UX.
- [ ] Repeat with different seq length distributions (avg out length=20, 50, 200); token mix heavily skews the relative ranking.
- [ ] Add real power-meter results for on-prem racks (measure real PUE, board-level power draw). Current watt assumptions are proxy.
- [ ] Integrate reserved capacity pricing scenarios (1/3/12 month) and recompute $/1k tokens for our standard workloads.
- [ ] Add per-route heuristics to Console (toggle cost vs energy vs latency) with recommended defaults.

Notes to self / rough provenance:
- Quick probe run on dev cluster; logs in /mnt/bench/2025-01-audit/ (raw CSVs). See JIRA-OPT-412 for the experiment plan and GH PR that added the A100 telemetry tag.
- This doc is intentionally informal — the experiment artifacts (sheets + raw CSV) will be linked into the Optimize canonical model once validated.

Questions / open items for PM/Eng review:
- What is the committed pricing expectation we should assume for Dedicated customers? That changes the thresholds.
- For Private (on-prem) customers, do we have standard PUE assumptions to run perf/W vs $/token tradeoffs?

Bottom line recommendation (short): adopt an instance-selection heuristic that defaults to A100 for cost-sensitive bulk generation, uses H100 for high-throughput/energy-sensitive cases, and exposes an L4/A10 fallback tier for dev/test and low-traffic tail routing. Add experiments above to validate quantization and reserved-price sensitivity before locking defaults.
